narrative:
The model determined that you have a 67.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were, in order of importance: your first-year class ranking, your undergraduate GPA, and your third-year class ranking. Your first-year ranking was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of 6 among students who were accepted, signaling that your early performance was unusually weak compared with successful applicants. This single factor hurt your chances more than any other.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.40 worked in the opposite direction. Because it sits noticeably above the 3.23 average of accepted students, the model viewed it as a positive signal that pulled the prediction back toward passing. However, this helpful effect was not large enough to overcome the other influences.

Your third-year ranking in the second decile also pushed toward failure, though less forcefully than your first-year standing. Again, this placed you well below the typical ranking of accepted students.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic trajectory, especially the weak early performance, made success on the bar exam uncertain. To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your class rank in the remaining years, consider a structured bar-preparation program, and retake the LSAT if possible to demonstrate improvement. These steps can materially change how a similar model evaluates you next time.
